steps.why: The sac gathers tears from both lids before they drain down.

steps.label: Nasolacrimal duct
steps.text: The nasolacrimal duct carries them down through the nasolacrimal canal.
steps.why: The duct runs down inside the bony canal of the skull toward the nose.

steps.label: Into the nose
steps.text: The tears empty into the nose below the lowest nasal concha.
steps.why: This last step is why crying gives you a runny nose, and why an eye drop can leave a taste in your throat.

distractors.text: The tears drain straight into the nasolacrimal duct from the surface of the eye.
distractors.why: Tears first enter the puncta and run through the canaliculi into the sac; the duct begins below the sac.

distractors.text: Lacrimal ducts carry them back into the lacrimal gland.
distractors.why: The ducts carry tears out of the gland onto the eye. Nothing returns tears to the gland.

error.text: They drain into openings at the outer corner of each lid.
error.why: The lacrimal puncta sit at the inner corner, near the nose, where blinking delivers the tears.

pathways.summary: Lacrimal gland, lacrimal ducts, across the eye, lacrimal puncta, canaliculi, lacrimal sac, nasolacrimal duct, nose. Tears are made at the upper outer corner and drain at the inner corner.

pathways.title: Phototransduction in a rod
pathways.intro: A rod sits in the dark, depolarized and releasing glutamate. Then a single photon arrives. Trace how light changes the rod’s signal.

steps.label: Retinal absorbs a photon
steps.text: Retinal in a rhodopsin molecule absorbs a photon.
steps.why: Light acts at only one step: the absorption by retinal.

steps.label: 11-cis to all-trans
steps.text: The kink in retinal straightens: 11-cis-retinal becomes all-trans-retinal.
steps.why: This photoisomerization is the only step that needs light; everything after it is chemistry.

steps.label: Rhodopsin becomes active
steps.text: The opsin changes shape, and rhodopsin becomes active.
steps.why: The shape change of retinal forces a shape change in the opsin around it.

steps.label: Transducin switched on
steps.text: Active rhodopsin switches on many molecules of the G protein transducin.
steps.why: Opsin is a G protein–coupled receptor protein, and one active rhodopsin activates dozens of transducins: the first amplification.

steps.label: Enzyme breaks down cGMP
steps.text: Transducin switches on an enzyme that breaks down cGMP.
steps.why: Each enzyme destroys many cGMP molecules: the second amplification.

steps.label: Cation channels close
steps.text: With less cGMP, the cation channels close, and the dark current stops.
steps.why: cGMP was holding those channels open; as it falls, they shut.

steps.label: Rod hyperpolarizes
steps.text: K+ still leaks out, so the rod hyperpolarizes from about −40 mV toward −70 mV.
steps.why: With Na+ no longer coming in, the outward K+ leak pulls the voltage down.

steps.label: Less glutamate released
steps.text: The hyperpolarized rod releases less glutamate onto its bipolar cells.
steps.why: Release depends on depolarization, so the signal of light is a drop in glutamate.

steps.label: Bipolar, ganglion cells act
steps.text: The bipolar cells respond to the change, and the ganglion cells change their firing.
steps.why: The change in glutamate is the message passed on toward the brain.

distractors.text: Active rhodopsin opens sodium channels directly, and the rod depolarizes.
distractors.why: Rhodopsin acts through a G protein, and light closes channels. The rod hyperpolarizes in light.

distractors.text: Active rhodopsin triggers action potentials in the rod’s axon.
distractors.why: Rods make no action potentials. They signal with graded changes in voltage and glutamate release.

error.text: cGMP rises and opens more cation channels, and the rod depolarizes.
error.why: Light lowers cGMP. The channels close, the dark current stops and the rod hyperpolarizes, the reverse of most sensory receptors.

pathways.summary: Light straightens retinal, rhodopsin activates transducin, and an enzyme destroys cGMP. The cGMP-held channels close, the dark current stops, the rod hyperpolarizes and its glutamate release falls. Two amplifying steps let one photon matter.

pathways.title: Focusing on something near
pathways.intro: You look up at a distant tree, then down at a text message on your phone. Trace how the lens changes shape to focus the near image.

steps.label: Near light spreads out
steps.text: Light from the nearby phone arrives spreading out, so it needs more bending than light from the tree.
steps.why: The problem to be solved comes first: a near object’s rays diverge.

steps.label: Oculomotor nerve fires
steps.text: Parasympathetic fibers of the oculomotor nerve fire.
steps.why: The near response is driven by the oculomotor nerve.

steps.label: Ciliary muscle contracts
steps.text: The ring of the ciliary muscle contracts, becomes smaller and moves in toward the lens.
steps.why: Because the ciliary muscle is a ring, contracting shrinks it.

steps.label: Zonule fibers go slack
steps.text: The zonule fibers that hold the lens go slack.
steps.why: With the ring closer to the lens, its threads no longer pull on the lens rim.

steps.label: Lens rounds up
steps.text: Released from tension, the elastic lens bulges into a rounder shape.
steps.why: The lens rounds up by its own elasticity when nothing stretches it.

steps.label: More bending
steps.text: The rounder lens bends light more.
steps.why: A more curved surface bends light more strongly.

steps.label: Image falls on the retina
steps.text: The near image comes to a focus on the retina, and the text is sharp.
steps.why: The extra bending brings the diverging rays together on the retina instead of behind it.

distractors.text: The zonule fibers tighten and squeeze the lens rounder.
distractors.why: Tight zonule fibers stretch the lens thin and flat. The lens rounds up when they go slack.

distractors.text: The cornea changes shape to add the bending.
distractors.why: The cornea’s power is fixed. Only the lens can change its bending.

error.text: The ciliary muscle relaxes, and the ring widens away from the lens.
error.why: That is the state for far vision. For near vision the ciliary muscle contracts and the ring shrinks toward the lens.

pathways.summary: For near vision the oculomotor nerve contracts the ciliary muscle, the zonule fibers go slack, and the elastic lens rounds up and bends light more. With age the lens stiffens and no longer rounds up: presbyopia.

pathways.title: Sound through the ear to the cortex
pathways.intro: A friend calls your name from across the room. Trace the sound from the air to your auditory cortex.

steps.label: Auricle funnels sound
steps.text: The auricle collects the sound waves and funnels them into the ear canal.
steps.why: The external ear is the entrance, and its folds help tell whether a sound is above or below you.

steps.label: Tympanic membrane vibrates
steps.text: The pressure waves vibrate the tympanic membrane at the end of the canal.
steps.why: The eardrum seals the canal from the middle ear and moves with the waves.

steps.label: Ossicles carry it across
steps.text: The malleus, incus and stapes carry the vibration across the middle ear, raising its pressure about 20-fold.
steps.why: The large eardrum and the lever of the ossicles concentrate the force onto the small oval window.

steps.label: Stapes rocks oval window
steps.text: The stapes rocks in the oval window and sets up pressure waves in the perilymph of the scala vestibuli.
steps.why: The oval window is where the air-borne vibration becomes a fluid wave.

steps.label: Basilar membrane vibrates
steps.text: The waves make the basilar membrane vibrate most at the place tuned to each frequency, while the round window bulges out.
steps.why: Fluid cannot be compressed, so each inward push of the stapes is matched at the round window, and the wave peaks at its own place.

steps.label: Stereocilia bend
steps.text: The tectorial membrane slides across the hair cells, bending their stereocilia back and forth.
steps.why: The hair cells ride on the basilar membrane under the tectorial membrane. The outer hair cells' tallest stereocilia are embedded in it; the inner hair cells' are bent by the fluid it drags.

steps.label: Hair cells release glutamate
steps.text: Channels open and close with each bend, and the hair cells release glutamate in rhythm with the sound.
steps.why: Bending opens mechanically gated channels, and K+ entering from endolymph depolarizes the cell.

steps.label: Cochlear nerve fires
steps.text: Sensory neurons with cell bodies in the spiral ganglion fire, in the cochlear branch of the vestibulocochlear nerve.
steps.why: The hair cell has no axon, so its sensory neuron carries the signal to the brain.

steps.label: Cochlear nuclei
steps.text: The axons synapse in the cochlear nuclei of the brainstem, on the same side.
steps.why: The first relay is on the same side as the ear.

steps.label: Superior olivary nuclei
steps.text: Signals from both ears meet in the superior olivary nuclei, which compare timing and loudness.
steps.why: This is the first place the two ears are compared, which is how you locate the sound.

steps.label: Inferior colliculus
steps.text: The signal climbs to the inferior colliculus of the midbrain.
steps.why: The inferior colliculus also turns your head toward a sudden sound.

steps.label: Medial geniculate nucleus
steps.text: It relays in the medial geniculate nucleus of the thalamus.
steps.why: Hearing, like vision and touch, relays in the thalamus.

steps.label: Primary auditory cortex
steps.text: It reaches the primary auditory cortex in the temporal lobe, and you hear your name.
steps.why: The cortex keeps the cochlea’s map of frequency, from low notes to high.

distractors.text: The stapes pushes on the round window, setting up pressure waves in the perilymph of the scala tympani.
distractors.why: The stapes sits in the oval window, which opens into the scala vestibuli. The round window at the end of the scala tympani bulges out to relieve the pressure.

distractors.text: The malleus reaches through the oval window and vibrates the hair cells of the spiral organ directly.
distractors.why: The ossicles never touch the hair cells. They move the fluid through the oval window, and the fluid moves the basilar membrane.

error.text: It relays in the lateral geniculate nucleus of the thalamus.
error.why: The lateral geniculate nucleus is the visual relay. Hearing relays in its medial neighbor, the medial geniculate nucleus.

pathways.summary: Air, bone, then fluid: the eardrum and ossicles deliver sound to the oval window, the basilar membrane sorts it by pitch, and bent stereocilia make hair cells release glutamate. The signal climbs through the cochlear nuclei, superior olives, inferior colliculus and medial geniculate nucleus to the temporal lobe, reaching both hemispheres from each ear.

pathways.title: How a hair cell turns a bend into a signal
pathways.intro: A sound pushes the basilar membrane upward, and the stereocilia of an inner hair cell bend toward their tallest member. Trace how that bend becomes a burst of action potentials.

steps.label: Bundle bends to the tallest
steps.text: The stereocilia bend toward the tallest stereocilium.
steps.why: The stimulus is a tiny deflection of the staircase-shaped bundle.

steps.label: Tip links stretch
steps.text: The tip links joining each stereocilium to its taller neighbor are stretched.
steps.why: Bending toward the tall side pulls the short tips away from their neighbors.

steps.label: Channels open
steps.text: The mechanically gated channels at the ends of the tip links open.
steps.why: Each tip link tugs its channel open, like a string on a trapdoor.

steps.label: K+ flows in
steps.text: K+ flows into the cell from the K+-rich endolymph around the stereocilia.
steps.why: Endolymph is high in K+ and about 80 mV positive, so both gradients push K+ into the cell.

steps.label: Hair cell depolarizes
steps.text: The hair cell depolarizes.
steps.why: Positive charge entering makes the inside less negative.

steps.label: Calcium channels open
steps.text: Voltage-gated Ca2+ channels at the base of the cell open, and Ca2+ enters.
steps.why: The depolarization spreads to the base, where the synapse is.

steps.label: More glutamate released
steps.text: Calcium triggers the release of more glutamate onto the sensory neuron.
steps.why: As at any chemical synapse, calcium entry triggers exocytosis of transmitter.

steps.label: Sensory neuron fires faster
steps.text: The cochlear sensory neuron fires faster than its resting rate.
steps.why: Because some channels are open at rest, the neuron has a background rate that can rise for one direction of bending and fall for the other.

distractors.text: K+ flows out of the cell into the endolymph, as in most cells.
distractors.why: Around the stereocilia the gradient is reversed: endolymph is K+-rich and positive, so K+ flows in and depolarizes the cell.

distractors.text: Na+ from the perilymph rushes in through voltage-gated sodium channels.
distractors.why: The stereocilia stand in endolymph, which is low in Na+. The current through the tip-link channels is carried mainly by K+.

error.text: The hair cell fires an action potential down its own axon to the brainstem.
error.why: A hair cell has no axon. It releases glutamate onto a sensory neuron, and that neuron carries the action potentials.

pathways.summary: Bending toward the tallest stereocilium stretches the tip links, opens channels, and lets K+ flow in from the endolymph. The cell depolarizes, Ca2+ enters at its base, more glutamate is released, and the sensory neuron fires faster. Bending the other way does the reverse.

pathways.title: Sympathetic pathway: spinal cord to effector
pathways.intro: You are nervous before an exam, and sweat breaks out on your palms. Trace the sympathetic signal from the spinal cord to a sweat gland in your palm.

steps.label: Lateral horn neuron fires
steps.text: A preganglionic neuron in the lateral horn of an upper thoracic segment fires.
steps.why: Sympathetic preganglionic cell bodies sit only in the lateral horn of T1–L2.

steps.label: Out the ventral root
steps.text: Its axon leaves the cord through the ventral root.
steps.why: Like all motor output, preganglionic axons leave through the ventral root.

steps.label: Into the spinal nerve
steps.text: It enters the spinal nerve for about a centimeter.
steps.why: The ventral root joins the dorsal root to form the spinal nerve just outside the cord.

steps.label: White ramus communicans
steps.text: It turns off into the white ramus communicans.
steps.why: The white ramus is the connecting branch into the chain, white because its preganglionic fibers are myelinated.

steps.label: Synapse in a chain ganglion
steps.text: It enters the sympathetic chain, climbs to a higher level, and synapses on a postganglionic neuron in a chain ganglion.
steps.why: The skin’s supply relays in the chain, and climbing the chain lets upper thoracic outflow reach the arm’s spinal nerves.

steps.label: Gray ramus communicans
steps.text: The unmyelinated postganglionic axon returns to a spinal nerve through a gray ramus communicans.
steps.why: Gray rami carry unmyelinated postganglionic fibers back out; every spinal nerve has one.

steps.label: Out along the arm’s nerves
steps.text: It rides out in the nerves of the arm to the skin of the palm.
steps.why: Postganglionic fibers travel with the spinal nerves to the skin and limbs.

steps.label: Sweat gland secretes
steps.text: Its varicosities release transmitter onto the sweat gland, which secretes sweat.
steps.why: The effector is a gland in the skin, reached only by sympathetic fibers.

distractors.text: It turns off into the gray ramus communicans.
distractors.why: Gray rami carry unmyelinated postganglionic fibers back out of the chain. Myelinated preganglionic fibers enter through the white ramus.

distractors.text: It runs through the dorsal root ganglion into the chain.
distractors.why: The dorsal root carries only sensory axons in. Preganglionic axons leave by the ventral root and reach the chain through the white ramus.

error.text: It passes through the chain without synapsing and runs in a splanchnic nerve to the celiac ganglion.
error.why: That is the route to the abdominal organs. Fibers for the skin synapse in the chain ganglia and return to the spinal nerves.

pathways.summary: Lateral horn, ventral root, spinal nerve, white ramus, chain ganglion (synapse), gray ramus, spinal nerve, effector. Two neurons, with the ganglion near the cord: a short preganglionic fiber and a long postganglionic one.

pathways.title: Sympathetic pathway through the adrenal medulla
pathways.intro: A car swerves toward you, and within seconds epinephrine pours into your blood. Trace the sympathetic route that releases it.

steps.label: Lateral horn neuron fires
steps.text: A preganglionic neuron in the lateral horn of a lower thoracic segment fires.
steps.why: Every sympathetic route starts with a preganglionic neuron in the lateral horn of T1–L2.

steps.label: Ventral root and white ramus
steps.text: Its axon leaves through the ventral root and enters the chain through the white ramus communicans.
steps.why: Preganglionic fibers reach the chain through the white rami.

steps.label: Through the chain, no synapse
steps.text: It passes through the chain ganglion without synapsing.
steps.why: Fibers bound for the abdomen do not relay in the chain.

steps.label: Splanchnic nerve
steps.text: It runs in a splanchnic nerve toward the celiac ganglion.
steps.why: Splanchnic nerves carry preganglionic fibers from the chain to the abdomen.

steps.label: Through the celiac ganglion
steps.text: It passes through the celiac ganglion without synapsing.
steps.why: Unlike most fibers arriving there, these have no second neuron to meet.

steps.label: Onto chromaffin cells
steps.text: It ends on chromaffin cells in the adrenal medulla and releases acetylcholine onto them.
steps.why: The chromaffin cells take the place of postganglionic neurons: same embryonic origin, but no axons.

steps.label: Epinephrine into the blood
steps.text: The chromaffin cells release epinephrine (about 80%) and norepinephrine into the blood.
steps.why: Without axons, the cells release their product into the blood, as an endocrine gland does.

steps.label: Reaches the whole body
steps.text: Epinephrine circulates to cells all over the body, including cells no sympathetic fiber touches, for a few minutes.
steps.why: As a hormone it reaches every tissue, and it lasts minutes after the nerve signal stops.

distractors.text: It synapses in the celiac ganglion on a postganglionic neuron whose axon reaches the adrenal medulla.
distractors.why: The adrenal medulla is the exception: preganglionic fibers reach it directly, with no postganglionic neuron.

distractors.text: It synapses in the chain ganglion, and a gray ramus carries the signal to the adrenal gland.
distractors.why: Gray rami return fibers to the spinal nerves for the skin and limbs. The adrenal route passes through the chain without synapsing.

error.text: The chromaffin cells send axons to the heart and release norepinephrine onto it.
error.why: Chromaffin cells have no axons. They release epinephrine and some norepinephrine into the blood, which carries them everywhere.

pathways.summary: Lateral horn, ventral root, white ramus, through the chain, splanchnic nerve, through the celiac ganglion, chromaffin cells, epinephrine into the blood. One neuron only: the adrenal medulla behaves like a sympathetic ganglion that secretes into the blood.

pathways.title: The pupillary light reflex as an autonomic reflex
pathways.intro: A doctor shines a penlight into your right eye, and both pupils narrow within a second. Trace the autonomic reflex arc.

steps.label: Retinal ganglion cells fire
steps.text: Light strikes the right retina, and retinal ganglion cells fire.
steps.why: The sensory side starts in the retina.

steps.label: Optic nerve
steps.text: Signals travel along the right optic nerve.
steps.why: The afferent pathway is the optic nerve.

steps.label: Pretectal nuclei, both sides
steps.text: They reach the pretectal nuclei of the midbrain on both sides.
steps.why: The midbrain is the integration center, and it shares the signal with both sides.

steps.label: Edinger–Westphal nuclei
steps.text: Each pretectal nucleus signals the parasympathetic nucleus of the oculomotor nerve (the Edinger–Westphal nucleus) on both sides.
steps.why: These nuclei hold the preganglionic parasympathetic neurons for the eye.

steps.label: Preganglionic fibers in III
steps.text: Preganglionic fibers run in both oculomotor nerves to the ciliary ganglia.
steps.why: The efferent side is the two-neuron chain; the preganglionic fiber is long.

steps.label: Short postganglionic fibers
steps.text: Short postganglionic fibers release acetylcholine onto muscarinic receptor proteins of the circular iris muscle.
steps.why: The terminal ganglion sits right behind the eye, so the postganglionic fibers are short.

steps.label: Both pupils narrow
steps.text: The circular muscle contracts, and both pupils narrow.
steps.why: The effector responds, and less light reaches each retina.

distractors.text: Preganglionic fibers leave the cord at T1 and climb the sympathetic chain to the eye.
distractors.why: That sympathetic route drives the dilator muscle, which widens the pupil in dim light.

distractors.text: Motor neurons in the facial nerve carry the command to the iris.
distractors.why: The facial nerve carries parasympathetic fibers to glands, not to the eye. The pupil’s narrowing travels in the oculomotor nerve.

error.text: Short postganglionic fibers release norepinephrine onto alpha-1 receptor proteins of the circular iris muscle.
error.why: Parasympathetic postganglionic neurons are cholinergic and act on muscarinic receptor proteins. Norepinephrine on alpha-1 contracts the dilator, which widens the pupil.

pathways.summary: Retina, optic nerve, pretectal nuclei, Edinger–Westphal nuclei, oculomotor nerves, ciliary ganglia, circular muscle. Because the midbrain sends the signal to both sides, one lit eye narrows both pupils, and one test checks the optic nerve, the midbrain and the oculomotor nerve.

pathways.title: Erythropoiesis: stem cell to erythrocyte
pathways.intro: A blood donor’s marrow replaces the red cells she gave. Trace one new red cell from the stem cell to a mature erythrocyte in her blood.

steps.label: Myeloid stem cell
steps.text: A myeloid stem cell in the red bone marrow commits to the red cell line.
steps.why: Every formed element descends from the hematopoietic stem cell; red cells come from its myeloid branch.

steps.label: Proerythroblast
steps.text: Driven by EPO, it becomes a proerythroblast.
steps.why: EPO binds receptor proteins on these early precursors, letting them survive and start maturing. Without EPO they die.

steps.label: Erythroblasts fill up
steps.text: Over several divisions, erythroblasts make hemoglobin until it fills their cytoplasm, while the nucleus shrinks.
steps.why: The divisions multiply the cells, and hemoglobin must be made while the cell still has its nucleus and ribosomes to make protein.

steps.label: Nucleus pushed out
steps.text: The cell pushes out its nucleus.
steps.why: Only once the cell is full of hemoglobin does it discard the nucleus, making room for more hemoglobin. From now on it cannot divide.

steps.label: Reticulocyte leaves marrow
steps.text: The cell, now a reticulocyte with a net of leftover ribosomes, leaves the marrow for the blood.
steps.why: The ribosomes remain for a day or two after the nucleus is gone, which is what stains as the fine net. Proerythroblast to reticulocyte takes about a week.

steps.label: Mature erythrocyte
steps.text: Within a day or two in the blood it loses its ribosomes and becomes a mature erythrocyte.
steps.why: Losing the ribosomes is the last step. That is why about 1% of red cells in a sample are reticulocytes: each spends about a day in the blood as one.

distractors.text: The cell divides once more into two mature erythrocytes.
distractors.why: Mature erythrocytes cannot divide. The step that turns an erythroblast into a reticulocyte is losing the nucleus.

distractors.text: The cell picks up a nucleus from a neighboring macrophage.
distractors.why: The cell loses its nucleus; it never gains one. The nucleus is thrown out to make room for hemoglobin.

distractors.text: The cell loses its ribosomes and becomes a mature erythrocyte inside the marrow.
distractors.why: Ribosomes are lost last, in the blood. A cell that still has them is a reticulocyte.

error.text: Erythroblasts push out their nucleus first, and only then start making hemoglobin.
error.why: Making hemoglobin needs the nucleus and ribosomes. Erythroblasts fill with hemoglobin first, and the nucleus is pushed out afterward.

pathways.summary: Myeloid stem cell, proerythroblast, erythroblasts filling with hemoglobin, nucleus pushed out, reticulocyte, mature erythrocyte. EPO drives the early stages; the whole trip takes about a week, plus a day or two as a reticulocyte in the blood.

pathways.title: Red blood cell life cycle and bilirubin
pathways.intro: A red cell has circulated for about 120 days. Follow it, and then its heme, until the pigment leaves your body.

steps.label: Cell ages
steps.text: The old red cell, unable to make new proteins, stiffens and collects marks of age on its surface.
steps.why: With no nucleus or ribosomes, a red cell cannot repair itself, so its membrane and enzymes wear out over about 120 days.

steps.label: Macrophage engulfs it
steps.text: A macrophage recognizes the old cell and engulfs it, mainly in blood-filtering organs and the liver.
steps.why: The marks of age are what the macrophage recognizes. Stiff cells are caught where blood filters slowly past macrophages.

steps.label: Globin, iron, heme split
steps.text: Inside the macrophage, hemoglobin is split into globin, iron and heme.
steps.why: Each part follows its own route: globin becomes amino acids for reuse, and iron goes to transferrin for the marrow or storage.

steps.label: Heme → bilirubin
steps.text: The heme ring is opened into green biliverdin, which is converted to yellow-orange bilirubin.
steps.why: The ring cannot be reused once its iron is gone, so it is opened and turned into a pigment for disposal.

steps.label: Carried on albumin
steps.text: Bilirubin leaves the macrophage and travels in the plasma bound to albumin.
steps.why: Unconjugated bilirubin dissolves poorly in water, so it rides on albumin, the plasma’s main carrier.

steps.label: Conjugated in the liver
steps.text: Liver cells take it up and conjugate it, making it water-soluble.
steps.why: Only a water-soluble form can be secreted in bile, and conjugation is what the liver adds.

steps.label: Out in bile
steps.text: The liver secretes conjugated bilirubin in bile, which drains into the intestine.
steps.why: Bile is the liver’s route out of the body for wastes it has made water-soluble.

steps.label: Stercobilin in feces
steps.text: Intestinal bacteria convert it to urobilinogen, and most becomes brown stercobilin in the feces.
steps.why: That is why feces are brown. A little urobilinogen is absorbed and leaves in urine as yellow urobilin.

distractors.text: The kidneys filter the bilirubin straight into urine.
distractors.why: Unconjugated bilirubin is bound to albumin and insoluble in water, so it cannot pass into urine. It must be conjugated by the liver first.

distractors.text: Liver cells rebuild the bilirubin into heme for new hemoglobin.
distractors.why: Heme without its iron cannot be reused. Liver cells conjugate bilirubin so it can be excreted.

distractors.text: The bone marrow stores the bilirubin until the next red cell is made.
distractors.why: Bilirubin is not stored for reuse; it is a waste pigment on its way out of the body.

error.text: Inside the macrophage, hemoglobin is split into globin, iron and heme, and the iron is excreted in urine.
error.why: Iron is recycled, not excreted: transferrin carries it back to the marrow or to storage. Each day macrophages recover about 20–25 mg, nearly all of what the marrow needs.

pathways.summary: Old red cells are engulfed by macrophages. Globin becomes amino acids, iron is recycled by transferrin, and heme becomes biliverdin, then bilirubin, which rides albumin to the liver, is conjugated, leaves in bile, and becomes stercobilin in feces (with a little urobilin in urine). A block at any point causes jaundice.

pathways.title: Hemostasis: spasm to fibrin
pathways.intro: You nick a small artery in your forearm on a sharp edge. Trace how the bleeding is stopped, from the tear to a firm clot. The steps start within seconds of each other and overlap.

steps.label: Wall tears
steps.text: The vessel wall tears, exposing collagen and tissue factor beneath the lining.
steps.why: Everything that follows is set off by what the tear exposes: collagen for platelets and tissue factor for clotting proteins.

steps.label: Vascular spasm
steps.text: Smooth muscle in the wall contracts: vascular spasm narrows the vessel.
steps.why: Direct injury, chemicals at the site and local nerve reflexes make the muscle contract at once. Slower flow lets platelets and clotting proteins build up instead of washing away.

steps.label: Platelets stick; TF starts
steps.text: Platelets stick to von Willebrand factor on exposed collagen. At the same time, plasma meets tissue factor, and tissue factor with VIIa makes a first trickle of thrombin.
steps.why: Both start from the tear itself. Tissue factor does not wait for platelets; initiation on tissue factor cells runs alongside platelet adhesion.

steps.label: Platelets activate
steps.text: Stuck platelets activate: they change shape, release ADP, serotonin and calcium, and make thromboxane A2.
steps.why: Binding to von Willebrand factor and collagen, and the trickle of thrombin, set off signals inside each platelet.

steps.label: Soft platelet plug
steps.text: ADP and thromboxane A2 activate passing platelets, which are bridged by fibrinogen into a soft plug.
steps.why: Activated platelets activate more platelets: positive feedback that builds the plug quickly, kept local by the healthy lining around it.

steps.label: Thrombin burst
steps.text: On the activated platelet surface, clotting factors make a burst of thrombin.
steps.why: The activated platelet surface is where IXa–VIIIa and Xa–Va work fastest, so the big burst needs the plug first.

steps.label: Fibrin mesh
steps.text: Thrombin cuts fibrinogen into fibrin, and XIIIa cross-links the threads through and around the plug: a firm clot.
steps.why: Fibrin is the end point of coagulation. Only the fibrin mesh holds against blood pressure in anything bigger than a small cut.

distractors.text: Platelets release their granules first, and only then is tissue factor exposed to start clotting.
distractors.why: Tissue factor sits in the vessel wall and is exposed by the tear itself. Clotting starts on it at the same time platelets stick, not after they release their granules.

distractors.text: Red blood cells stick to the collagen and form the plug.
distractors.why: Red cells do not stick to collagen; platelets do, through von Willebrand factor. Red cells are only trapped later in the fibrin mesh.

distractors.text: Fibrin threads form first, and platelets then stick to them.
distractors.why: Fibrin comes last, from the burst of thrombin on activated platelets. The platelets must stick and activate before that burst.

error.text: On the activated platelet surface, antithrombin makes a burst of thrombin.
error.why: Antithrombin does the opposite: it inactivates thrombin and Xa. The burst comes from IXa–VIIIa activating X and Xa–Va converting prothrombin to thrombin.

pathways.summary: A tear exposes collagen and tissue factor. The vessel constricts; platelets stick while tissue factor starts clotting; activated platelets recruit more into a soft plug; their surface hosts a burst of thrombin; and thrombin turns fibrinogen into a cross-linked fibrin mesh. The steps overlap, and the plug alone seals only the smallest breaks.

pathways.title: Coagulation cascade overview
pathways.intro: Clotting in your body happens on cell surfaces: the cell-based model. Trace the clotting factors from the moment a vessel tears to a cross-linked fibrin mesh.

steps.label: Plasma meets tissue factor
steps.text: A tear brings plasma into contact with tissue factor on fibroblasts and smooth muscle cells in the wall, as platelets begin to stick.
steps.why: Blood never touches tissue factor while the lining is intact, so the tear itself is the trigger.

steps.label: TF–VIIa activates X, IX
steps.text: Factor VIIa, which circulates already active, binds tissue factor, and the pair activates factors X and IX.
steps.why: VIIa can do little until it binds tissue factor, so this step can only follow the exposure.

steps.label: A trickle of thrombin
steps.text: Xa, with its cofactor Va, turns a little prothrombin into a little thrombin.
steps.why: This first thrombin is too little to make a clot. Within seconds, an inhibitor switches the tissue factor–VIIa pair off.

steps.label: Platelets, V, VIII, XI primed
steps.text: The trickle of thrombin activates the platelets in the plug and activates factors V, VIII and XI.
steps.why: Thrombin is a strong platelet activator. Priming the cofactors prepares the platelet surface for the burst.

steps.label: Platelet surface ready
steps.text: Activated platelets flip negatively charged phospholipid to their outer face, where calcium ions anchor clotting factors.
steps.why: The factors work fast only when held on a membrane surface, and calcium is what holds them.

steps.label: IXa–VIIIa activates X
steps.text: On the platelet surface, IXa pairs with VIIIa and activates X at a high rate.
steps.why: With tissue factor–VIIa switched off, this pair takes over. It is the step missing in hemophilia A (VIII) and B (IX).

steps.label: Thrombin burst
steps.text: Xa pairs with Va and converts prothrombin to thrombin in a large burst.
steps.why: Now the enzymes sit together on one surface in large numbers, and each activated enzyme activates many molecules of the next: amplification.

steps.label: Fibrinogen → fibrin
steps.text: Thrombin cuts soluble fibrinogen into fibrin, which links up into insoluble threads.
steps.why: This is the end point that everything before it was building toward: a large amount of thrombin in the right place.

steps.label: XIIIa cross-links
steps.text: Factor XIIIa, activated by thrombin, cross-links the fibrin threads into a strong mesh that traps red cells.
steps.why: Fibrin threads must exist before they can be cross-linked, so this comes last.

distractors.text: On the platelet surface, factor XIIa activates XI, which starts the whole cascade.
distractors.why: That is the start of the lab model’s intrinsic pathway in a glass tube. In your body, factor XII is not needed: people who lack it do not bleed.

distractors.text: Tissue factor with VIIa keeps activating X at a high rate on the platelet surface.
distractors.why: The tissue factor–VIIa pair is switched off within seconds by an inhibitor protein. The burst depends on IXa with VIIIa.

distractors.text: Plasmin activates X on the platelet surface.
distractors.why: Plasmin breaks fibrin down during fibrinolysis. It plays no part in building the clot.

error.text: Xa, with its cofactor Va, turns prothrombin into enough thrombin to clot the blood at once.
error.why: The first thrombin made on tissue factor cells is only a trickle, too little to clot. Its job is to activate platelets and cofactors so that the burst can happen on the platelet surface.

pathways.summary: Initiation on tissue factor cells makes a trickle of thrombin; amplification uses it to activate platelets and factors V, VIII and XI; propagation on the platelet surface (IXa–VIIIa, then Xa–Va) makes a burst of thrombin, which makes cross-linked fibrin. For your exam, the same factors are also taught as the extrinsic (tissue factor and VIIa), intrinsic (XII, XI, IX, VIII) and common (X, V, II, I, XIII) pathways.

pathways.title: The lab model: intrinsic and common pathways
pathways.intro: Exams and the aPTT test still use the lab model. Plasma is added to a tube with a negatively charged contact surface, phospholipid and calcium. Trace the intrinsic and common pathways to a clot in the tube.

steps.label: Contact activates XII
steps.text: Contact with the negatively charged surface activates factor XII.
steps.why: Everything the intrinsic pathway needs is in the blood; contact with a surface like glass is its trigger.

steps.label: XIIa activates XI
steps.text: XIIa activates XI.
steps.why: Each activated factor is an enzyme that cuts and activates the next in line.

steps.label: XIa activates IX
steps.text: XIa activates IX.
steps.why: The cascade passes the signal on, amplifying it at each step.

steps.label: IXa + VIIIa activate X
steps.text: IXa, with its cofactor VIIIa, activates X.
steps.why: This is where the intrinsic pathway joins the common pathway. The extrinsic pathway (tissue factor with VIIa) activates X too, which is why both meet here.

steps.label: Prothrombin → thrombin
steps.text: Xa, with Va and calcium, converts prothrombin to thrombin.
steps.why: Activating X starts the common pathway, shared by both routes.

steps.label: Fibrinogen → fibrin
steps.text: Thrombin cuts fibrinogen into fibrin.
steps.why: Thrombin is the enzyme that makes fibrin, so fibrin comes after it.

steps.label: XIIIa cross-links
steps.text: XIIIa cross-links the fibrin, and the sample clots.
steps.why: Cross-linking needs fibrin to exist first. The time to reach a clot is the aPTT, normally about 25–35 seconds.

distractors.text: XIa activates X directly, without IX.
distractors.why: XIa’s target is IX. It is IXa, with its cofactor VIIIa, that activates X, which is why missing VIII or IX lengthens the aPTT.

distractors.text: IXa activates VIII, which cuts prothrombin directly.
distractors.why: VIII is a cofactor, not the enzyme that makes thrombin. IXa with VIIIa activates X, and Xa converts prothrombin.

distractors.text: Calcium is removed with citrate so that X can be activated.
distractors.why: Citrate is used to stop the sample clotting before the test. Calcium is added back, because the factors need it.

error.text: Thrombin cuts fibrin into fibrinogen.
error.why: It is the other way round. Fibrinogen is the soluble plasma protein; thrombin cuts it into fibrin, the insoluble threads.

pathways.summary: Intrinsic: XII, XI, IX (with VIII), meeting the extrinsic pathway (tissue factor with VII) at X. Common: X (with V), prothrombin to thrombin, fibrinogen to fibrin, XIII cross-links. The aPTT tests the intrinsic and common pathways; the PT tests the extrinsic and common. In your body factor XII is not needed; this is the model for reading tests and for exams.

pathways.title: An ABO transfusion reaction
pathways.intro: A type O patient is given a unit of type A red cells by mistake. Trace what happens in her blood.

steps.label: A cells enter O plasma
steps.text: Red cells carrying A antigen enter plasma that holds anti-A.
steps.why: Everyone with type O blood has anti-A and anti-B in their plasma from infancy, without any earlier transfusion.

steps.label: Anti-A binds
steps.text: Her anti-A binds the A antigens on the donor cells within seconds.
steps.why: The antibodies are already there, so no time is needed to make them; binding is immediate.

steps.label: Agglutination
steps.text: Each antibody bridges A antigens on two cells, clumping the donor cells.
steps.why: Each antibody has several binding sites, so it can link antigens on neighboring cells into visible clumps.

steps.label: Donor cells burst
steps.text: Antibodies bound to the cells switch on plasma proteins that punch holes, and the donor cells burst.
steps.why: Hemolysis follows binding, because it is the bound antibodies that switch on the hole-punching proteins.

steps.label: Free hemoglobin
steps.text: Hemoglobin released into the plasma spills into the urine, and its heme is turned into bilirubin.
steps.why: The hemoglobin could only escape once the cells burst.

steps.label: Fever, falling pressure
steps.text: Signals released by the antibody attack cause fever, chills, pain and a fall in blood pressure.
steps.why: These signals come from the attack, so they follow binding; the fall in pressure can lead to shock.

distractors.text: Fibrin threads trap the donor cells in a clot.
distractors.why: That is coagulation. The clumping in a transfusion reaction is agglutination: antibodies linking cells by their surface antigens.

distractors.text: Her immune system spends two weeks making new anti-A.
distractors.why: Anti-A is already present in type O plasma. That delay is the pattern for a first exposure to the Rh antigen, not ABO.

distractors.text: The donor’s anti-B clumps her red cells.
distractors.why: Type A plasma has anti-B, but type O red cells carry no B antigen, and packed cells carry little plasma anyway. The danger is her antibodies against the donor cells.

error.text: Red cells carrying A antigen enter her plasma, which has no antibodies until she is exposed.
error.why: Unlike Rh, ABO antibodies are present from a few months of age without any exposure to donor blood, probably because bacteria in the intestine carry look-alike sugar chains. That is why an ABO mismatch reacts at once.

pathways.summary: Donor antigen meets antibodies already in the plasma, which bind at once, agglutinate the cells and switch on hemolysis. Free hemoglobin reaches the urine and becomes bilirubin, and the attack causes fever and falling blood pressure. Stop the transfusion at once.

pathways.title: How Rh antibodies harm a later pregnancy
pathways.intro: An Rh-negative mother is not given anti-D immune globulin. Trace how her first Rh-positive baby leads to hemolytic disease in the next.

steps.label: Rh+ fetus, Rh− mother
steps.text: An Rh-negative mother carries an Rh-positive fetus, which inherited a D gene from its father.
steps.why: The disease needs a mother without the D antigen and a fetus with it.

steps.label: Fetal cells enter at birth
steps.text: At delivery, some fetal red cells enter the mother’s blood.
steps.why: The two bloods normally stay apart during pregnancy; mixing happens mostly at birth.

steps.label: Mother makes anti-D
steps.text: Over the following weeks her immune system makes anti-D. The first baby, already born, is unharmed.
steps.why: Anti-D forms only after exposure, and slowly, so it arrives too late to harm the first baby.

steps.label: Anti-D crosses
steps.text: In a later Rh-positive pregnancy, her anti-D crosses from her blood to the fetus.
steps.why: Her anti-D is of the kind that crosses to the fetus, and once she is sensitized it is always there.

steps.label: Fetal red cells destroyed
steps.text: Anti-D binds the fetus’s red cells, which are destroyed, causing anemia and a flood of erythroblasts.
steps.why: The fetal marrow and liver respond to the anemia by releasing immature, still-nucleated cells.

steps.label: Jaundice after birth
steps.text: After birth, the baby’s immature liver cannot keep up, and bilirubin climbs fast.
steps.why: Before birth the mother’s liver cleared the bilirubin; after birth the baby must do it alone.

distractors.text: The first baby is destroyed by anti-D that the mother had from infancy.
distractors.why: Rh-negative people have no anti-D until they are exposed. The first baby is usually unharmed.

distractors.text: She is given anti-D immune globulin, which clears the fetal cells.
distractors.why: That is the prevention, and it would stop the disease. In this pathway she was not given it, so she made her own anti-D.

distractors.text: The fetus makes anti-D against its mother’s red cells.
distractors.why: The mother’s cells lack the D antigen, so there is nothing for anti-D to bind; the harm runs from mother to fetus.

error.text: In a later Rh-positive pregnancy, her anti-A and anti-B cross to the fetus and destroy its cells.
error.why: Most anti-A and anti-B are too large to cross to the fetus. The severe disease comes from anti-D, which does cross.

pathways.summary: Rh-positive fetal cells enter an Rh-negative mother at the first birth; she makes anti-D over weeks; in the next Rh-positive pregnancy her anti-D crosses and destroys fetal red cells, causing anemia, erythroblasts in the blood and severe jaundice after birth. Anti-D immune globulin at about 28 weeks and within 72 hours of delivery clears fetal cells before she can make her own anti-D.

pathways.title: The cAMP cascade: water-soluble hormone to cell response
pathways.intro: Epinephrine reaches a liver cell and, within seconds, glycogen starts to break down. Trace the signal from the hormone outside the cell to the response inside, and then how it is switched off.

steps.label: Hormone binds
steps.text: Epinephrine, the first messenger, binds its receptor protein in the plasma membrane.
steps.why: A water-soluble hormone cannot cross the lipid bilayer, so the signal starts at a receptor protein on the outer surface.

steps.label: G protein on
steps.text: The receptor protein changes shape and switches on a G protein on the inner face of the membrane.
steps.why: The shape change reaches through the membrane. The G protein is the relay between the receptor protein and the enzyme.

steps.label: Adenylyl cyclase on
steps.text: The G protein switches on adenylyl cyclase, an enzyme in the membrane.
steps.why: Adenylyl cyclase is the enzyme that makes the second messenger, so it must be switched on before any cAMP appears.

steps.label: ATP to cAMP
steps.text: Adenylyl cyclase turns many ATP molecules into cyclic AMP (cAMP), the second messenger.
steps.why: Each active enzyme makes many cAMP molecules: the signal is amplified inside the cell.

steps.label: Protein kinase A on
steps.text: cAMP binds and switches on protein kinase A.
steps.why: Protein kinase A stays off until cAMP binds it, so it comes after cAMP has built up.

steps.label: Proteins phosphorylated
steps.text: Protein kinase A phosphorylates target proteins, including other kinases: a phosphorylation cascade.
steps.why: Each kinase adds phosphate groups to many proteins, amplifying the signal again.

steps.label: Cell responds
steps.text: The phosphorylated enzymes change their activity, and the liver cell breaks glycogen down to glucose.
steps.why: Phosphorylation changes an enzyme’s shape and so its activity. Which proteins a cell contains decides what the response is.

steps.label: Signal switched off
steps.text: Phosphodiesterase breaks cAMP down to AMP, phosphatases remove the phosphates, and the G protein switches itself off.
steps.why: The response lasts only while new cAMP is being made. Once the hormone lets go, these enzymes return the cell to rest.

distractors.text: The G protein carries the hormone into the nucleus.
distractors.why: The hormone never enters the cell. The G protein passes the signal to a membrane enzyme.

distractors.text: Phosphodiesterase makes cAMP from ATP.
distractors.why: Phosphodiesterase breaks cAMP down; adenylyl cyclase makes it.

distractors.text: The G protein opens calcium channels in the endoplasmic reticulum, releasing calcium as the second messenger.
distractors.why: That is the calcium pathway, where a different enzyme makes IP3. In the cAMP pathway the G protein switches on adenylyl cyclase.

error.text: cAMP enters the nucleus and switches on transcription of new genes.
error.why: cAMP acts in the cytosol by switching on protein kinase A, which changes proteins the cell already has. Changing transcription directly is how lipid-soluble hormones act.

pathways.summary: Hormone, receptor protein, G protein, adenylyl cyclase, cAMP, protein kinase A, phosphorylated proteins, response. Every step multiplies the signal, and phosphodiesterase, phosphatases and the G protein’s own switch end it.

pathways.title: Lipid-soluble hormone to new protein
pathways.intro: A woman starts a steroid tablet for a skin disease. Nothing visible happens that day, but her rash settles over two or three days. Trace the hormone from the blood to the change in her cells.

steps.label: Leaves carrier protein
steps.text: The steroid comes off its carrier protein in the plasma and leaves the capillary as free hormone.
steps.why: Only free hormone can leave the blood and reach target cells; bound hormone is a reservoir.

steps.label: Crosses the membrane
steps.text: The free hormone diffuses through the phospholipid bilayer of the target cell.
steps.why: A lipid-soluble hormone dissolves in the bilayer, so it needs no surface receptor protein to get in.

steps.label: Binds receptor protein
steps.text: It binds its receptor protein in the cytosol or the nucleus; a cytosolic complex then moves into the nucleus.
steps.why: Only target cells carry this intracellular receptor protein, so only they respond.

steps.label: Binds DNA
steps.text: The hormone–receptor complex binds a hormone response element, a short DNA sequence near the genes it controls.
steps.why: The complex must reach the DNA before it can change which genes are read.

steps.label: Transcription changes
steps.text: The complex acts as a transcription factor, switching transcription of those genes on or off.
steps.why: Binding the hormone response element lets the complex speed or block the reading of nearby genes into mRNA.

steps.label: mRNA translated
steps.text: The new mRNA leaves the nucleus and is translated into new proteins.
steps.why: Proteins can be made only after their mRNA exists, which is why the response takes hours.

steps.label: Cell’s activity changes
steps.text: The new enzymes, channels or transporters change what the cell does, and the effect lasts as long as the proteins do.
steps.why: The response is carried by proteins the cell did not have before, so it starts slowly and lasts for days.

distractors.text: The hormone–receptor complex moves back to the plasma membrane and switches on a G protein on its inner face.
distractors.why: G proteins relay signals from membrane receptor proteins for water-soluble hormones. This complex acts on DNA.

distractors.text: The hormone is broken down to release a second messenger.
distractors.why: No second messenger is needed: the hormone–receptor complex itself acts on DNA.

distractors.text: The complex moves the cell’s existing enzymes to the membrane.
distractors.why: The lipid-soluble route makes new proteins; it does not act by moving old ones.

error.text: The free hormone binds a receptor protein on the outer surface of the plasma membrane and stays outside the cell.
error.why: That is how water-soluble hormones act. A steroid dissolves in the lipid bilayer and binds its receptor protein inside the cell.

pathways.summary: Free hormone, through the membrane, intracellular receptor protein, hormone response element, transcription, translation, new proteins. Making new proteins takes hours, and the proteins last, so these hormones act slowly and for a long time.

pathways.title: Posterior pituitary: making and releasing ADH
pathways.intro: After a salty meal, ADH appears in your blood within minutes. Follow one ADH molecule from where it is made to the blood.

steps.label: Made in cell body
steps.text: A neuron of the supraoptic nucleus in the hypothalamus makes ADH as a peptide and packs it into vesicles.
steps.why: ADH is made by hypothalamic neurons, not by the pituitary gland, so the story starts in the cell body.

steps.label: Carried down the axon
steps.text: The vesicles travel down the axon, through the infundibulum, to axon terminals in the posterior pituitary.
steps.why: The posterior pituitary is made of these axons, so the hormone reaches it by moving along them.

steps.label: Stored in terminals
steps.text: The vesicles are stored in the axon terminals until the neuron fires.
steps.why: The posterior pituitary makes no hormone; it stores what arrives.

steps.label: Neuron fires
steps.text: Osmoreceptors excite the neuron, and action potentials run down the axon to the terminals.
steps.why: Release is set by nerve signals, so an action potential must arrive before any ADH leaves.

steps.label: Calcium enters
steps.text: Voltage-gated calcium channels open in the terminals and calcium enters.
steps.why: As at a synapse, calcium entry is the trigger for exocytosis.

steps.label: Exocytosis
steps.text: The vesicles fuse with the membrane and release ADH by exocytosis.
steps.why: Calcium makes the vesicles fuse, emptying their hormone outside the cell.

steps.label: Into the blood
steps.text: ADH diffuses into capillaries in the posterior pituitary and is carried away in the blood.
steps.why: Only in the blood is it a hormone, reaching the kidneys and vessels far away.

distractors.text: The ADH is released into the first capillary network and carried by the hypophyseal portal veins to the anterior pituitary.
distractors.why: The portal veins carry releasing and inhibiting hormones to the anterior lobe. ADH travels inside axons to the posterior lobe.

distractors.text: Cells of the posterior pituitary copy the hormone and make more of it.
distractors.why: The posterior pituitary makes no hormones; it only stores and releases ADH and oxytocin.

distractors.text: The ADH is released into the cerebrospinal fluid.
distractors.why: ADH is carried down axons and released into the blood.

error.text: ADH diffuses out through the membrane of the axon terminal, because it is lipid-soluble.
error.why: ADH is a peptide, water-soluble, and cannot cross the bilayer. It leaves by exocytosis of its vesicles.

pathways.summary: Made in the hypothalamus, carried down the axon, stored in the posterior pituitary, released by exocytosis when the neuron fires. Neurons that release hormones: nerve signals decide when ADH enters the blood.

pathways.title: Making and releasing thyroid hormone
pathways.intro: Iodine from a pinch of iodized salt ends up, weeks later, as part of a T4 molecule in your blood. Trace the steps inside a thyroid follicle.

steps.label: Iodide trapped
steps.text: A cotransporter in the follicular cell’s membrane pulls iodide in from the blood along with sodium.
steps.why: Iodide must be concentrated inside the cell before any can be attached; this secondary active transport uses the sodium gradient.

steps.label: Thyroglobulin made
steps.text: The follicular cell makes thyroglobulin and releases it into the thyroid colloid by exocytosis.
steps.why: The hormones are built on tyrosines within thyroglobulin, so the protein must be in the colloid first.

steps.label: Iodine attached
steps.text: At the cell’s inner surface, an enzyme converts iodide to a reactive form and attaches it to tyrosines in thyroglobulin.
steps.why: Iodination happens where iodide and thyroglobulin meet, at the edge of the colloid.

steps.label: Tyrosines coupled
steps.text: Pairs of iodinated tyrosines join, still part of thyroglobulin, to make T4 and T3.
steps.why: Coupling needs tyrosines that already carry iodine.

steps.label: Stored in colloid
steps.text: The finished hormones stay attached to thyroglobulin in the colloid, enough for two to three months.
steps.why: Storage comes before release; the gland holds far more hormone than any other.

steps.label: Colloid taken back
steps.text: When TSH arrives, the follicular cells take colloid back in by endocytosis.
steps.why: The hormone is still attached to thyroglobulin, so the cell must bring the colloid inside to free it.

steps.label: Lysosomes free T4, T3
steps.text: Lysosomes digest the thyroglobulin, freeing T4 and T3.
steps.why: Digesting the protein backbone releases the hormones from it.

steps.label: Into the blood
steps.text: T4 and T3 leave the cell into the capillaries, where most binds carrier proteins.
steps.why: Once free of thyroglobulin, the hormones can leave for the blood and reach every tissue.

distractors.text: TSH carries iodine into the colloid.
distractors.why: TSH is a signal that speeds each step; it does not carry iodine.

distractors.text: The follicular cell builds T4 inside its own cytosol and releases it straight into the capillaries as soon as each molecule is made.
distractors.why: The hormones are built on thyroglobulin in the colloid and stored there before release.

distractors.text: Parafollicular cells attach iodine to calcitonin.
distractors.why: Parafollicular cells make calcitonin, which has no iodine. Follicular cells build T4 and T3.

error.text: The finished hormones are stored for a few minutes inside vesicles in the follicular cells.
error.why: Thyroid hormone is stored outside the cells, in the colloid, attached to thyroglobulin, and the store lasts two to three months.

pathways.summary: Trap iodide, make thyroglobulin, attach iodine, couple, store in the colloid, take the colloid back, digest it, release T4 and T3. TSH speeds every step.

pathways.title: How a beta cell releases insulin
pathways.intro: After a meal, blood glucose climbs and insulin rises within minutes. Trace what happens inside one beta cell.

steps.label: Glucose enters
steps.text: Blood glucose rises, and glucose enters the beta cell by facilitated diffusion through glucose carrier proteins.
steps.why: More glucose outside means more glucose inside; the beta cell senses glucose by taking it in.

steps.label: ATP rises
steps.text: The cell breaks the glucose down in cellular respiration, and its ATP level rises.
steps.why: The cell reads the glucose level as its ATP level, so glucose must be broken down first.

steps.label: K+ channels close
steps.text: ATP binds and closes ATP-sensitive potassium channels in the plasma membrane.
steps.why: These channels respond to ATP, so they close only once ATP has risen.

steps.label: Membrane depolarizes
steps.text: Fewer potassium ions leak out, so the membrane depolarizes.
steps.why: Potassium leaving normally holds the membrane negative; blocking the leak lets it become less negative.

steps.label: Calcium flows in
steps.text: Depolarization opens voltage-gated calcium channels, and calcium ions flow in.
steps.why: Voltage-gated channels open only after the membrane has depolarized.

steps.label: Insulin released
steps.text: Calcium triggers exocytosis of vesicles packed with insulin, which enters the islet’s capillaries.
steps.why: As at a synapse, calcium entry makes the vesicles fuse and empty.

distractors.text: ATP opens more potassium channels, so the cell hyperpolarizes.
distractors.why: ATP closes these channels. Opening more would hyperpolarize the cell and stop insulin release.

distractors.text: A sensory nerve tells the beta cell that glucose is high.
distractors.why: The beta cell is its own sensor; no nerve is needed.

distractors.text: Glucose binds a receptor protein on the surface and switches on cAMP.
distractors.why: The beta cell senses glucose by breaking it down and reading the rise in ATP.

error.text: Depolarization opens voltage-gated sodium channels, and sodium triggers exocytosis of insulin.
error.why: The trigger for exocytosis is calcium, entering through voltage-gated calcium channels.

pathways.summary: Glucose in, ATP up, potassium channels shut, the membrane depolarizes, calcium enters, insulin out. As glucose falls, ATP falls, the channels reopen and release slows: the loop turns itself off.

pathways.title: The renin–angiotensin–aldosterone system
pathways.intro: After a day of vomiting, a man’s blood volume and blood pressure are low, and his kidneys make very little urine. Trace the hormone chain that makes them keep salt and water.

steps.label: Pressure falls
steps.text: Blood pressure in the kidney’s small arteries falls, and sympathetic nerves fire more.
steps.why: The chain starts with what the kidney senses: lower pressure, sympathetic signals through beta-1 receptor proteins, and less salt flowing past its sensing cells.

steps.label: Kidney releases renin
steps.text: Specialized kidney cells release renin, an enzyme, into the blood.
steps.why: Renin is the first product. How much is released sets how fast the whole chain runs.

steps.label: Angiotensin I made
steps.text: Renin cuts angiotensinogen, a protein the liver releases all the time, into angiotensin I.
steps.why: Angiotensinogen is always in the plasma, so renin is the step that decides how much angiotensin I is made.

steps.label: ACE makes angiotensin II
steps.text: Angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE), on the inner lining of blood vessels and most plentiful in the lungs, converts angiotensin I into angiotensin II.
steps.why: Angiotensin I does very little itself; ACE turns it into the active hormone.

steps.label: Aldosterone released
steps.text: Angiotensin II makes the zona glomerulosa of the adrenal cortex release aldosterone.
steps.why: The adrenal step comes after angiotensin II, its main volume signal. Angiotensin II also constricts small arteries and raises ADH and thirst.

steps.label: New channels and pumps
steps.text: Aldosterone makes cells of the last stretch of the kidney’s tubules build more sodium channels and sodium–potassium pumps.
steps.why: Aldosterone is a steroid: it acts by making new proteins, so this step takes hours.

steps.label: Sodium kept, potassium lost
steps.text: More sodium is reabsorbed into the blood and more potassium is secreted into the urine.
steps.why: The new channels and pumps move the ions; potassium leaves as sodium is taken back.

steps.label: Water follows
steps.text: Water follows the sodium by osmosis, as long as ADH has made the tubes permeable, and blood volume rises.
steps.why: Water moves only after the sodium has moved, so volume recovers last.

steps.label: Renin falls
steps.text: As volume and pressure recover, the kidney releases less renin and the chain winds down.
steps.why: The response removes its own stimulus: negative feedback.

distractors.text: The liver converts angiotensin I into renin.
distractors.why: The liver supplies angiotensinogen. Renin comes from the kidney and acts before angiotensin I exists.

distractors.text: Angiotensin I acts directly on the adrenal cortex.
distractors.why: Angiotensin I does very little itself; it must first be converted to angiotensin II.

distractors.text: Angiotensin I travels to the adrenal medulla, whose chromaffin cells convert it into aldosterone and release it into the blood within seconds, before any enzyme acts.
distractors.why: Aldosterone is a steroid made from cholesterol by the zona glomerulosa of the cortex. It is not made from angiotensin.

error.text: More potassium is reabsorbed into the blood and more sodium is secreted into the urine.
error.why: That is backward. Aldosterone makes the kidney keep sodium and lose potassium, which is why a person on an ACE blocker tends to keep more potassium.

pathways.summary: Low pressure, renin, angiotensinogen to angiotensin I, ACE to angiotensin II, aldosterone, new channels and pumps, sodium kept and potassium lost, water follows, volume restored, renin falls. Every product travels in the blood, linking kidney, liver, lungs and adrenal cortex.

pathways.title: The hypothalamic–pituitary–adrenal axis
pathways.intro: A hiker breaks her ankle on a remote trail. Hours later, still waiting for rescue, her cortisol is several times its usual level. Trace how the stress reaches her adrenal cortex, and how the rise is limited.

steps.label: Stress sensed
steps.text: Pain and fear of the injury act on the hypothalamus.
steps.why: Physical and psychological stress both reach the hypothalamus, which is where the axis starts.

steps.label: CRH released
steps.text: Hypothalamic neurons release corticotropin-releasing hormone (CRH) into the hypophyseal portal system.
steps.why: The hypothalamus controls the anterior pituitary with hormones, not nerves, so it releases CRH into the portal blood.

steps.label: Portal veins
steps.text: The portal veins carry CRH, undiluted, down the infundibulum to the anterior pituitary.
steps.why: The portal system delivers CRH straight to the pituitary before it could be diluted in the whole circulation.

steps.label: ACTH released
steps.text: CRH makes cells of the anterior pituitary release ACTH into the blood.
steps.why: ACTH is the tropic hormone; it must be released before the adrenal cortex is driven.

steps.label: Zona fasciculata
steps.text: ACTH binds receptor proteins on zona fasciculata cells, which make and release cortisol within minutes.
steps.why: The adrenal cortex answers only after ACTH reaches it in the blood.

steps.label: Cortisol acts
steps.text: Cortisol raises blood glucose by driving gluconeogenesis and breaking down muscle protein, and damps inflammation.
steps.why: Cortisol acts on target tissues once it is in the blood; as a steroid, its effects build over hours.

steps.label: Feedback brakes CRH, ACTH
steps.text: Cortisol inhibits CRH release by the hypothalamus and ACTH release by the pituitary.
steps.why: Long-loop negative feedback limits the rise, although strong stress can override it.

distractors.text: CRH acts directly on the adrenal cortex to release cortisol.
distractors.why: CRH reaches only the anterior pituitary through the portal veins. ACTH carries the signal to the adrenal cortex.

distractors.text: The posterior pituitary releases ACTH down the axons of the hypothalamus.
distractors.why: ACTH comes from the anterior pituitary. The posterior lobe releases only ADH and oxytocin.

distractors.text: Sympathetic fibers carry the signal to the adrenal cortex.
distractors.why: Sympathetic fibers drive the adrenal medulla. The cortex answers to ACTH in the blood.

error.text: Cortisol stimulates more CRH and ACTH release, so the rise keeps growing.
error.why: Cortisol inhibits CRH and ACTH: negative feedback. That is also why steroid drugs suppress the axis and must be tapered.

pathways.summary: Stress, hypothalamus, CRH through the portal system, anterior pituitary, ACTH in the blood, zona fasciculata, cortisol, targets, and cortisol braking CRH and ACTH. A three-gland axis held by negative feedback.

pathways.title: Darkness to melatonin
pathways.intro: Evening falls and the room goes dark. Two or three hours before bedtime, melatonin starts to climb in your blood. Trace the pathway from your eyes to the pineal gland, and how light shuts it off.

steps.label: Retinal ganglion cells
steps.text: A small set of retinal ganglion cells containing melanopsin sense light, and in darkness they fall quiet.
steps.why: These cells carry light information, not images; darkness is signaled by their silence.

steps.label: Suprachiasmatic nucleus
steps.text: Their axons leave the visual pathway at the optic chiasm and reach the suprachiasmatic nucleus of the hypothalamus.
steps.why: The SCN, the master clock, combines the light signal with its own daily rhythm.

steps.label: Down the spinal cord
steps.text: From the hypothalamus, the signal runs down into the spinal cord.
steps.why: The pineal gland is controlled by the sympathetic system, whose preganglionic neurons are in the spinal cord.

steps.label: Superior cervical ganglion
steps.text: Sympathetic fibers leave the cord and relay in the superior cervical ganglion of the sympathetic chain.
steps.why: The postganglionic neurons that reach the head sit in this ganglion.

steps.label: Back up to the pineal
steps.text: Postganglionic sympathetic fibers run back up to the pineal gland.
steps.why: The signal must travel back into the skull to reach its target.

steps.label: Norepinephrine released
steps.text: At night, the fibers release norepinephrine onto pinealocytes.
steps.why: The pathway is active in darkness, so norepinephrine release is highest at night.

steps.label: Melatonin released
steps.text: Pinealocytes make melatonin from serotonin and release it into the blood.
steps.why: Norepinephrine is the signal that switches melatonin production on.

distractors.text: The optic nerve carries the signal straight to the pineal gland.
distractors.why: No direct nerve reaches the pineal gland from the eye. The signal goes through the SCN and the sympathetic chain.

distractors.text: The parasympathetic vagus nerve carries the signal to the pineal gland.
distractors.why: The pineal gland’s drive is sympathetic, from the superior cervical ganglion.

distractors.text: The anterior pituitary releases a tropic hormone into the blood, which reaches the pineal gland and makes it release melatonin.
distractors.why: The pineal gland is controlled by nerves, not by a pituitary hormone.

error.text: In bright light, the fibers release the most norepinephrine onto pinealocytes.
error.why: Light shuts the pathway down. Norepinephrine, and so melatonin, is released in darkness, and light stops it within minutes.

pathways.summary: Eye, SCN, spinal cord, superior cervical ganglion, sympathetic fibers, norepinephrine, pinealocytes, melatonin. At night, as timed by the SCN, the pathway runs; light turns it off within minutes. Evening light and screens also reset the SCN clock itself later.

pathways.title: Lymph flow from tissue to vein
pathways.intro: A splinter in your left foot lets bacteria into the tissue. Trace the fluid around it from the moment it enters the lymphatic system until it is back in your blood.

steps.label: Lymphatic capillary
steps.text: Interstitial fluid pushes the overlapping endothelial flaps inward and enters a blind-ended lymphatic capillary, becoming lymph.
steps.why: Entry comes first: the flaps open only when pressure outside is higher than inside, so fluid, protein and bacteria can get in but not back out.

steps.label: Collecting vessels
steps.text: Valved collecting vessels carry the lymph up the leg, pushed by their own smooth muscle and by the calf muscles.
steps.why: Lymphatic capillaries join into collecting vessels. Their one-way valves turn each squeeze into flow toward the heart.

steps.label: Afferent vessels to a node
steps.text: Afferent lymphatic vessels deliver the lymph into lymph nodes behind the knee and in the groin.
steps.why: Collecting vessels pass through lymph nodes before they merge, so lymph is filtered before it can reach the blood.

steps.label: Node sinuses
steps.text: The lymph trickles slowly through the sinuses, where macrophages engulf the bacteria and lymphocytes meet their antigens.
steps.why: Inside the node, the many afferent vessels and the wide maze of sinuses slow the lymph, giving macrophages time to clear it.

steps.label: Efferent vessel
steps.text: Lymph leaves each node through an efferent lymphatic vessel at the hilum.
steps.why: Lymph leaves only at the hilum, the indented side of the node, through one or two efferent vessels, after it has crossed the cortex and medulla.

steps.label: Left lumbar trunk
steps.text: Vessels from the leg merge into the left lumbar trunk.
steps.why: Collecting vessels leaving the nodes merge into large trunks named for the region they drain; the lumbar trunks drain the legs.

steps.label: Cisterna chyli
steps.text: The lumbar trunk empties into the cisterna chyli in front of the first two lumbar vertebrae.
steps.why: The cisterna chyli is the sac where the thoracic duct begins, receiving the lumbar and intestinal trunks.

steps.label: Thoracic duct
steps.text: The lymph climbs the thoracic duct in front of the spine, through the chest.
steps.why: The thoracic duct drains about three quarters of the body, including both legs, so lymph from the left foot takes this route.

steps.label: Left venous junction
steps.text: It empties into the blood where the left internal jugular vein meets the left subclavian vein, and travels on to the superior vena cava.
steps.why: The duct ends at the left venous junction, returning the filtered fluid and protein to the blood near the heart.

distractors.text: The lymph flows straight through the node in seconds, since nothing there acts on it before it leaves.
distractors.why: Lymph is slowed on purpose. Filtering by macrophages and lymphocytes is the whole point of passing through a node.

distractors.text: Blood capillaries in the node add fluid to the lymph, so more lymph leaves the node than entered it.
distractors.why: The reverse happens: blood capillaries in the node take back water, so less lymph leaves than entered, richer in lymphocytes.

distractors.text: The lymph enters the spleen, where red pulp macrophages remove the bacteria before it moves on.
distractors.why: The spleen has no afferent lymphatic vessels. It filters blood, not lymph.

error.text: It empties into the blood where the right internal jugular vein meets the right subclavian vein.
error.why: That junction receives the right lymphatic duct, which drains only the right arm, the right side of the chest and the right side of the head and neck. Lymph from the left foot travels in the thoracic duct to the left venous junction.

pathways.summary: Lymphatic capillary, collecting vessels, afferent vessels, node sinuses, efferent vessel, lumbar trunk, cisterna chyli, thoracic duct, left venous junction. Roughly 8 L of fluid a day enters lymph in the tissues; the nodes return up to half of it to the blood directly, so about 3 to 4 L (the classic exam figure is about 3 L) reaches the veins through the ducts.

pathways.title: The inflammatory response
pathways.intro: You cut your thumb on a dirty garden tool. Within minutes the edges redden; within hours they swell and fill with neutrophils; days later the cut is clean. Put the steps of inflammation in order.

steps.label: Alarm signals released
steps.text: Mast cells release histamine, damaged cells release prostaglandins, and macrophages whose pattern recognition receptor proteins bind the bacteria release cytokines.
steps.why: Everything that follows is driven by these chemical messengers, so their release comes first.

steps.label: Arterioles dilate
steps.text: Histamine and prostaglandins dilate the arterioles, so more blood flows in: redness and heat.
steps.why: The messengers act on the nearest vessels first, widening them within minutes.

steps.label: Vessels leak
steps.text: Capillary and venule endothelial cells pull apart, and plasma with its proteins leaks out: swelling.
steps.why: The same messengers open gaps in the vessel walls, letting complement, antibodies and clotting proteins reach the tissue.

steps.label: Leukocytes roll and stick
steps.text: Cytokines make the venule walls sticky; leukocytes in the slowed blood roll along the wall, then stop and hold tight.
steps.why: Blood has slowed in the widened vessels, and adhesion proteins on the endothelium catch passing leukocytes.

steps.label: Diapedesis
steps.text: Each leukocyte squeezes between two endothelial cells and out into the tissue.
steps.why: A leukocyte must first be held against the wall before it can squeeze through it.

steps.label: Chemotaxis
steps.text: The leukocytes crawl up the gradient of chemokines, complement fragments and bacterial products to the bacteria.
steps.why: Once in the tissue, the cell has to find the microbes, and it follows the rising concentration of attractants.

steps.label: Phagocytes kill
steps.text: Neutrophils, then macrophages, engulf the bacteria and kill them with lysosomal enzymes and the oxidative burst.
steps.why: Killing needs the phagocytes to have arrived at the microbes.

steps.label: Pus forms
steps.text: Neutrophils die within a day or two; dead cells, microbes, debris and leaked plasma collect as pus.
steps.why: Pus is what is left after neutrophils have done their work and died at the site.

steps.label: Resolution and repair
steps.text: Macrophages engulf the dying neutrophils and switch to signals that end inflammation and start tissue repair.
steps.why: Repair can begin only once the microbes are gone and the debris is cleared.

distractors.text: Each leukocyte bursts on the endothelium, releasing its granules into the blood.
distractors.why: Leukocytes leave the blood intact. They squeeze between endothelial cells and do their work in the tissue.

distractors.text: Each leukocyte is pumped out through the lymphatic capillaries into the tissue.
distractors.why: Lymphatic capillaries carry fluid away from the tissue, not leukocytes into it. Leukocytes leave the blood by diapedesis.

distractors.text: Each leukocyte waits in the venule until the bacteria reach the bloodstream.
distractors.why: Leukocytes leave the venule and go to the bacteria in the tissue, which is how an infection is kept local.

error.text: Histamine and prostaglandins constrict the arterioles, so less blood flows in: the site turns pale and cool.
error.why: Inflammatory messengers dilate the arterioles. The extra blood flow is what makes an inflamed area red and hot.

pathways.summary: Alarm signals, vasodilation, leak, rolling and sticking, diapedesis, chemotaxis, phagocytosis, pus, repair. The same order runs whether the trigger is bacteria in a cut or a sprain; messengers drive both the vessel changes and the arrival of leukocytes.

pathways.title: How a phagocyte kills
pathways.intro: A neutrophil has left a venule near an infected cut. Put the steps by which it finds and kills one bacterium in order.

steps.label: Chemotaxis
steps.text: The neutrophil crawls toward the bacterium, following the rising concentration of attracting chemicals.
steps.why: A phagocyte must reach its target before it can do anything to it.

steps.label: Binding
steps.text: It binds the bacterium, directly through pattern recognition receptor proteins or through complement (C3b) coating it.
steps.why: Engulfing needs a firm grip first; coating by C3b (opsonization) makes that grip much easier.

steps.label: Engulfing
steps.text: Its membrane flows around the bacterium and closes it into a vesicle.
steps.why: Once the bacterium is gripped, the membrane can wrap it.

steps.label: Fusion with lysosomes
steps.text: The vesicle fuses with lysosomes and granules, which pour in digestive enzymes, lysozyme and defensins.
steps.why: The weapons are stored separately in lysosomes and granules, so they must be delivered into the vesicle.

steps.label: Oxidative burst
steps.text: Superoxide made from oxygen by an enzyme in the vesicle membrane becomes hydrogen peroxide, and a granule enzyme delivered by the fusion turns it into hypochlorous acid.
steps.why: Hypochlorous acid, the strongest of these weapons, needs the granule enzyme, so it forms only after the granules have fused with the vesicle. Made inside the closed vesicle, these chemicals kill the trapped bacterium without harming the cell.

distractors.text: It releases a pore-forming protein onto the bacterium without touching it.
distractors.why: Releasing pore-forming granules onto a target is how NK cells kill infected body cells. A neutrophil grips a bacterium and engulfs it.

distractors.text: It waits for antibody-producing cells to arrive before it can act at all.
distractors.why: Neutrophils act within hours, long before antibodies are made on a first infection. They bind microbes directly or through complement.

error.text: The phagocyte uses the extra oxygen it takes up to make more ATP, which powers the enzymes that digest the bacterium.
error.why: The oxygen in the oxidative burst is used to make weapons (superoxide, hydrogen peroxide, hypochlorous acid), not ATP. That is why a phagocyte’s oxygen use jumps as it kills.

pathways.summary: Find, bind, engulf, fuse with lysosomes, kill with the oxidative burst. In chronic granulomatous disease the burst enzyme is faulty, so phagocytes engulf bacteria but cannot kill many of them.
